title: The Old Tent and the Final Sacrifice
overview: The writer compares Israel's old tent worship and animal sacrifices with the death of Jesus, arguing that his single offering of himself does what the yearly rituals could only point toward.

parts.label: The old tent and its rooms (vv. 1-5)
parts.note: The first covenant, God's binding agreement with Israel through Moses, came with a portable worship tent split into two rooms by a curtain. The inner room held the gold-covered chest called the ark, with keepsakes from the desert years inside and a gold lid where blood was sprinkled to cover the people's wrongs.

parts.label: Only one man, once a year (vv. 6-10)
parts.note: Priests served daily in the outer room, but only the high priest went into the inner room, on the yearly Day of Atonement, and always carrying sacrificial blood. The writer reads this closed door as a sign that open access to God had not yet come, and that such rituals cleaned people outwardly without settling the conscience.

parts.label: A better priest, a better room (vv. 11-14)
parts.note: The writer pictures Jesus as a high priest who entered God's own presence in heaven, offering his own life instead of an animal's. If animal blood and the ashes of a sacrificed young cow could make people ritually clean, he argues, Christ's death can clean the conscience itself.

parts.label: Why a death was needed (vv. 15-22)
parts.note: The Greek word for covenant can also mean a will, and the writer seems to use both senses: a will only takes effect after a death. He then recalls Moses sprinkling blood on the scroll, the people and the tent to seal the first covenant, since under that law forgiveness came through a life given.

parts.label: Once, not year after year (vv. 23-28)
parts.note: The earthly tent was only a copy of the heavenly reality, and its priest had to repeat the ritual every year with blood not his own. Christ, the writer says, offered himself once, just as each person dies once, and will appear again not to deal with sin but to bring final rescue to those waiting for him.

disagreement: Scholars and Christians differ on whether verses 16 and 17 really mean a will or a covenant sealed by death, and on whether the heavenly tent is meant as an actual place or as a picture of God's own presence.
think: What do you think it would take for a person to feel truly clear of something they deeply regret?
